scope: 1954 postarmistice statecraft: alliance, aid, currency, NNSC, force control, reconstruction
source_family: U.S. Department of State, Foreign Relations of the United States, 1952-1954, Korea, vol. XV part 2

findings: Mutual Defense Treaty entered into force 1954-11-17 by exchange of ratifications
Agreed Minute linked up to $700m FY1955 military/economic programs to ROK undertakings
ROK forces total 720,000 and continued UNC operational control were part of the arrangement
U.S. policy explicitly sought both ROK strength and restraint against unilateral northern military action
economic program disputes included exchange rate, procurement sources including Japan, and implementation cooperation
U.S. sought Swiss/Swedish withdrawal path to remove Polish/Czech NNSC teams without openly breaking armistice machinery
Won Yong-duk ultimatum was treated as a risk to the diplomatic approach
Rhee threatened action against Polish/Czech NNSC personnel if allied action did not occur within roughly a week or ten days
Sohn Won-il said he had no advance notice of Won Yong-duk's move
Briggs/Hull reported Sohn's indication that Won acted under Rhee's personal orders; this remains a contemporaneous diplomatic observation, not an ROK order document
Sixteen participant states discussed a coordinated approach to Swiss and Swedish NNSC members
the episode was multilateral, not solely bilateral Rhee-U.S. diplomacy
CINCUNC was instructed to maintain armistice, build ROK security, and seek ROK compliance
authorized ROK force structure included 20 army divisions plus marine/navy/air ceilings
CINCUNC also held field responsibility for integrated Korean economic aid under the 1953 presidential assignment
U.S. NSC discussed Rhee's cutoff of hwan advances and chose not to settle immediately
shows currency dispute was treated as strategic alliance management, not a narrow accounting matter
ROK stopped making hwan available except at 180:1 for U.S. forces and Korean employees
U.S. position used 254:1 for June-August drawings; dispute traced to unresolved February 1953 understanding

corrections_and_adversarial_results: Mutual Defense Treaty signature in 1953 must be separated from entry into force on 1954-11-17.
Alliance consolidation was not a single treaty event: treaty, Agreed Minute, operational control, force ceilings, aid, currency and NNSC disputes formed a negotiated package.
ROK military expansion and U.S. restraint policy coexisted; describing 1954 only as alliance strengthening misses the containment-of-ally dimension.
NNSC conflict was not reducible to Rhee alone; Won Yong-duk, Sohn Won-il, UNC commanders, U.S. diplomats and the sixteen participant states had distinct roles.
The statement that Won acted under Rhee's personal orders is preserved as Sohn-to-Briggs/Hull contemporaneous reporting, not upgraded to a directly authenticated Korean presidential order.
Economic aid was conditional and contested, not an unconditional transfer; exchange rate and procurement rules were core bargaining issues.
U.S. troop redeployment and ROK force expansion occurred together, so abandonment and militarization narratives require joint modeling.
Operational control was a legal-institutional restraint mechanism and should not be collapsed into generic alliance language.
NNSC removal proposals were constrained by armistice legality and allied diplomacy; unilateral expulsion and negotiated withdrawal were competing courses.
FRUS is an official U.S. documentary series and supplies U.S./allied provenance; Korean cabinet, presidential and National Assembly records remain necessary for symmetric attribution.
